title: Cultivating Amid Freedom from Thought

inline.s: (From Dream Journey Collection · Instructions to Shen Dajie)

“The two practices of Chan and Pure Land are originally not two dharmas; Master Yongming pointed this out long ago. Chan is fundamentally free from thought — this is certain. Yet the highest grade of the highest grade of rebirth in the Pure Land has never not been attained through cultivation within freedom from thought. If one recites the Buddha’s name to the point of single-mindedness without confusion, how could any thought remain? Though these two are not two, when it comes to getting down to work, there is indeed a difference of skillful and clumsy. Among practices, to direct the mind through inquiry is the subtlest and most intimate.”

These two practices, the Chan school and the Pure Land school, are originally not two dharmas. Master Yongming pointed this out long ago. Chan practice is indeed founded on freedom from thought, yet those who seek the highest grade of the highest grade of rebirth in the Pure Land school have never failed to cultivate within freedom from thought. If one recites the Buddha’s name to the point of single-mindedness without confusion, what thought could remain? Although the methods of the Chan and Pure Land practices are fundamentally not two dharmas, when it comes to getting down to work, there is nonetheless a distinction of skillful and clumsy. Among the practices, directing the mind through inquiry is the subtlest and most intimate.

[To the point of single-mindedness without confusion, how could any thought remain?] The “single-mindedness without confusion” spoken of here refers to the single-mindedness of principle — the ultimate single-mindedness. [The single-mindedness of principle] Master Ouyi said:
“The single-mindedness of practice
(single-mindedness of practice)
means distinctness and clarity, without dullness or scattering. The single-mindedness of principle
(single-mindedness of principle)
means tacitly according with the unborn and clearly penetrating one’s own nature.”
(From the Lingfeng School Discourses
Casual Talks in the Brahma Room). For details, see
the article “The Single-Mindedness of Practice and the Single-Mindedness of Principle”

“If at the time of inquiry one dwells in the non-arising of a single thought, yet speaks of reciting the Buddha’s name, then a thought arises again. In this way they become two separate things. The recitation should be done precisely at the point of inquiry-and-recitation, fused into a single thread, so that it does not arise and yet arises, and arising is itself non-arising. Only this is the genuine practice of Yongjia’s ‘dual flow of clarity and stillness.’ Why is this? If, in inquiry, one raises the huatou to block the mind-root, requiring that not a single thought arise — though this is the work of inquiry, the ancients called it ‘hugging the mooring post while rowing.’ That very thought of requiring non-arising is itself an arising; how could it be true non-arising?”

If at the time of inquiry one dwells in the non-arising of a single thought, yet recites the Buddha’s name, then a thought arises again. In this way, inquiry and recitation become two separate things. Therefore, the recitation should be done precisely at the point of inquiry-and-recitation (reciting without thought), fusing inquiry and recitation into a single thing (forging them into one thread), so that it (the thought) does not arise and yet arises, and arising is itself non-arising. Only this is the genuine practice of Master Yongjia’s balanced holding of clarity and stillness. Why is this? Because when, in inquiry, one raises the huatou to block the mind-root, requiring that not a single thought arise — though this is spoken of as doing the work of inquiry — the ancients called it ‘hugging the mooring post while rowing’ (a metaphor: while demanding no-thought, one is at the same time raising a thought). Here, that very thought of requiring the thought not to arise is itself the arising of a thought; how could it be true non-arising of thought?

[Reciting without thought] To recite the Buddha’s name with no-thought (the non-arising of a single thought) is the recollection of the Buddha of true reality, the recollection of the dharmakāya Buddha. (For details, see
the article “Reciting Without Thought”
.) [Recollection of the Buddha of true reality] To recollect the Buddha by means of ultimate emptiness and the dharma of non-existence. In the Buddha Store Sutra, the Buddha said:

“Śāriputra, what is called recollection of the Buddha? Seeing non-existence is called recollection of the Buddha. Śāriputra, the Buddhas are immeasurable, inconceivable, and beyond reckoning; for this reason, seeing non-existence is called recollection of the Buddha. The real is without discrimination, and the Buddhas are without discrimination; for this reason it is said that to recollect without discrimination is recollection of the Buddha. Again, seeing the true character of all dharmas is called seeing the Buddha. What is called the true character of all dharmas? It is that all dharmas are ultimately empty and non-existent. By means of this ultimately empty and non-existent dharma one recollects the Buddha. Again, in such a dharma, not even a small thought can be obtained — this
(this)

is called recollection of the Buddha. Śāriputra, this dharma of recollecting the Buddha cuts off the path of language, transcends all thoughts, and cannot be obtained as thought — this is called recollection of the Buddha. Śāriputra, all thoughts are of the character of quiescent extinction. To accord with this dharma is called the cultivation of recollecting the Buddha. One should not recollect the Buddha by way of form. Why? To recollect form is to grasp characteristics, and greed for flavor is consciousness. Without form, without color, without conditions, without nature — this is called recollection of the Buddha. Therefore you should know: to be without discrimination, without grasping and without rejecting, is true recollection of the Buddha.” “Recollection of the Buddha is called the breaking of all wholesome and unwholesome discernment; to be without discernment, without discursive thought, still and imageless, is called recollection of the Buddha. Why? One should not use discernment to recollect the Buddhas; to be without discernment and without discursive thought is called pure recollection of the Buddha. In this recollection there is not even the subtle karmic activity of mind upon mind, how much less the karma of body and speech!” “These dharmas are all empty, without substance or nature; one cannot recollect a single characteristic — what is called the signless — this is called true recollection of the Buddha. What is called the unborn and unceasing, the signless and unconditioned.” “The anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi of all Buddhas is entirely without thought and without recollection.”

[Discernment (jueguan)] Newly translated as “vitarka and vicāra,” formerly translated as “discernment.” Coarse reflection is called “discernment (jue),” fine reflection is called “discernment (guan)”; both can disturb the settled mind. [Yongjia’s dual flow of clarity and stillness] “Xingxing” (clarity) means alertness and vigilance. The “dual flow of clarity and stillness” means being both alert (clarity) and free of a single thought (stillness). Master Yongjia said:
“Clarity with stillness is right, clarity with delusive thought is wrong; stillness with clarity is right, stillness with unknowing is wrong.”
Here “unknowing” means dullness and obscurity.
[Hugging the mooring post while rowing] Hugging the post means tying the wooden boat to the shore post to keep it from drifting; rowing means making the boat leave the shore and move forward.

“As for reciting the Buddha’s name, if one hangs a single utterance of the Buddha’s name in the mind and never forgets it, thought after thought, how could that be true single-mindedness without confusion? The ancients taught people to investigate the living phrase, not the dead phrase — precisely to see, at the very point of arising, the meaning of non-arising. As a sutra says: ‘Only he who sees the instant realizes the unborn.’ With this one phrase, inquiry and recitation can at once become a single thread.”

Just as with reciting the Buddha’s name, if one hangs a single utterance of the Buddha’s name in the mind and never forgets it, thought after thought, how could that be the ultimate single-mindedness without confusion? The ancients taught people to investigate the living phrase, not the dead phrase — precisely to see, at the very point of arising, the meaning of non-arising. As a sutra says: ‘Only he who sees the instant (who sees the subtle arising and ceasing) realizes the unborn.’ With this one phrase, inquiry and recitation can at once become a single thing.

[Living phrase and dead phrase] A term used in the Chan school. A meaningless phrase through which the path of thought cannot pass is called a living phrase; a meaningful phrase through which the path of thought can pass is called a dead phrase. The Record of the Forest says:
“Chan Master Dongshan Chu said: where there is speech within speech, it is called a dead phrase; where there is no speech within speech, it is called a living phrase.”
[Instant (kṣaṇa)]

A transliteration of a Sanskrit word. In translation: a thought-moment, that is, the interval in which a single thought arises. It is commonly used to denote an extremely short time. [Only he who sees the instant realizes the unborn] Only he who sees the subtle arising and ceasing realizes the unborn. Master Hanshan said:

“Guishan said: ‘For a person of today to understand his own mind all at once in a single thought is called awakening. Then, using what has been awakened to, he purifies away the residual karmic streaming consciousness — this is called cultivation.’ Now, the streaming consciousness refers to the subtle arising and ceasing, which is the instantaneous mind.”
(From Dream Journey Collection

Instructions to Chan Practitioner Lingjian Zhizhi of the West Hall, Jingshan) [Subtle arising and ceasing] The subtle arising, ceasing, and flowing of the discriminating mind is the character of the ālayavijñāna.

“Practitioner of the Way, listen well! In inquiry and recitation it is easy to fall into confusion and error; this must not be neglected. How is inquiry itself recitation, and recitation itself inquiry? In inquiry now, take the single phrase ‘Amitābha’ as the huatou and do the work of scrutinizing. Lay down all at once your own body and mind, your world, and all your former worldly truths, customary words, and Buddhist views and understanding.”

Practitioner of the Way (a cultivator of the Way), listen carefully! In inquiry and recitation it is easiest to go wrong; this must not be neglected. How is inquiry itself recitation, and recitation itself inquiry? In inquiry now, take the single phrase ‘Amitābha’ as the huatou and do the work of scrutinizing. Lay down all at once your own body and mind, your world, and all your former worldly truths, customary words, and Buddhist views and understanding.
[Taking the single phrase ‘Amitābha’ as the huatou and doing the work of scrutinizing] This is inquiry-and-recitation. For details, see
the article “Inquiry and Recitation”

. [Laying down all at once your own body and mind, your world, and all your former worldly truths, customary words, and Buddhist views and understanding] Inquiry means investigating apart from mind, intention, and consciousness, so one must first lay down all at once one’s own body and mind, one’s world, and all former worldly truths, customary words, and Buddhist views and understanding. [Investigating apart from mind, intention, and consciousness] Accumulation is called mind; deliberation is called intention; discrimination is called consciousness. Among “mind, intention, and consciousness,” mind refers to the eighth consciousness (ālayavijñāna), intention to the seventh consciousness (manas), and consciousness to the remaining six consciousnesses (eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind consciousness). “Investigating apart from mind, intention, and consciousness” means investigating apart from the operation of the discriminating mind. (On the operation of the discriminating mind, see
the article “Mind, Self-Nature, and the Tathāgatagarbha”

, the section “The Process of the Discriminating Mind’s Operation.”) “Investigating apart from mind, intention, and consciousness” is also what the Sixth Patriarch said in the Platform Sutra: “I tell all practitioners of the Way: in your work you must use intention; do not, within the gate of the Mahāyāna, grasp after the wisdom of birth and death.” (Translation: I inform you practitioners of the Way that in doing the work you must use intention (manas); do not be cultivating the Mahāyāna gate yet use the discriminating mind to do the work.) [Intention] That is, the manas, also called the mind-root. The characteristic of the manas is perpetual deliberation, giving rise to the discriminating mind. [In your work you must use intention] The manas perpetually deliberates, clings to mental objects, and constantly gives rise to the discriminating mind and delusive thoughts; therefore investigating Chan is to use the manas to investigate, blocking the flow of delusive thoughts so that they do not proceed, and right at the point where they do not proceed, to look for the original face. Master Hanshan said: “What is above is the ordinary pincers-and-hammer that Old Man Dahui used; its meaning is only to have you use the huatou to block the flow of delusive thoughts beneath the mind-root so that they do not proceed, and right at the point of non-proceeding, to look for the original face. It is not teaching you to ponder over a public case, to raise the doubt-sensation and seek an answer.” (From Dream Journey Collection
Instructions on the Essentials of Chan Inquiry) [The wisdom of birth and death] The discriminating mind.

“Then, from within that empty, still silence, forcefully raise a single utterance of ‘Amitābha Buddha,’ distinct and clear. Just as it is raised, look straight at it and scrutinize: who is it that is reciting the Buddha’s name? Bring the doubt-sensation to bear, scrutinizing again and again, doubting again and again, like the donkey gazing into the well.”

Then, from within that empty, still silence, forcefully raise a single utterance of ‘Amitābha Buddha,’ distinct and clear. Just as it is raised, look straight at it and scrutinize: who is it that is reciting the Buddha’s name? Bring the doubt-sensation to bear (the “doubt-sensation” spoken of here is to concentrate the spirit and scrutinize: who is it that recites the Buddha’s name?), scrutinizing again and again (the “scrutinizing” spoken of here is gazing and investigating), doubting again and again, like the donkey gazing into the well.
[Like the donkey gazing into the well] A metaphor for gazing and investigating beyond the discrimination of feeling and consciousness. The Record of Caoshan says:
“The master
(Chan Master Caoshan Benji Yuanzheng)
asked the Elder De: ‘The Buddha’s true dharmakāya is like empty space; it responds to things and manifests forms, like the moon in the water. How would you explain the principle of responding
(how should this principle be explained)
?’ De said: ‘Like the donkey gazing into the well.’ The master said: ‘You have only said eighty percent of it.’ De said: ‘And what do you say, Venerable
(Venerable, how would you put it)
?’ The master said: ‘Like the well gazing at the donkey.’”

“Gaze and gaze, doubt and doubt, until you doubt to the point where the path of mind and thought is cut off, like a silver mountain or an iron wall, with no place to turn or draw breath. At that moment, when you suddenly bump against it, the true meaning of the unborn will abruptly appear before you. Then the whole body streams with sweat, as if waking from a great dream. Only at this point do you believe that arising is itself non-arising, and non-arising is itself arising; that inquiry is itself recitation, and recitation is itself inquiry. Looking back, you will realize for the first time that all along it was like searching for Chang’an while standing inside the Hanyuan Palace.”

Gaze and gaze, doubt and doubt, until you doubt to the point where the path of mind and thought is cut off, like a silver mountain or an iron wall, with no place to turn or draw breath. At that moment, when you suddenly bump against it, the true meaning of the unborn will abruptly appear before you. Then the whole body streams with sweat, as if waking from a great dream. Only at this point do you believe that arising is itself non-arising, and non-arising is itself arising; that inquiry is itself recitation, and recitation is itself inquiry. Looking back, you will realize for the first time that everything you had done all along was like searching for Chang’an while standing inside the Hanyuan Palace.

[Like searching for Chang’an inside the Hanyuan Palace] The Hanyuan Palace was the main hall of the imperial palace in Chang’an, the capital of the Tang dynasty. “Like searching for Chang’an inside the Hanyuan Palace” is a metaphor for being originally a Buddha and yet seeking to become a Buddha.

“In doing the work this way, what is most to be feared is the mind wanting to attain awakening. The very moment there is a mind that wants awakening, it is a board blocking the way. Just keep working straight on, without reckoning the amount of work. Even when you reach the point where you cannot go on, rouse your spirits and begin anew.”

In doing the work this way, what is most to be feared is the mind waiting for awakening. The very moment there is a mind waiting for awakening, it is a board blocking the way. Therefore, just keep working straight on, without reckoning the amount of work. Even when you reach the point where you cannot go on, be sure to rouse your spirits and begin anew.
[Board blocking the way] A board that blocks the view, a metaphor for the mind that wants awakening being an obstacle that blocks the seeing of the Way.

“Moreover, you must never crave the profound and wondrous. Even if for a moment a single thought rests and there is stillness and joy, you must never regard this as a good thing — you must simply spit it out. Never use the profound words and wondrous sayings of the Buddhas and Patriarchs as proof, taking them for the Buddha-dharma; and never fall into the shell of having nothing to do, taking that as attainment.”

Moreover, you must never crave the profound and wondrous. Even if for a moment a single thought rests and there is stillness and joy, you must never regard this as a good thing — you must simply cast this joyful mind aside (spit it out). Never use the profound words and wondrous sayings of the Buddhas and Patriarchs as proof, taking them for the Buddha-dharma; and never fall into the shell of having nothing to do, taking that as attainment.

[Never use the profound words and wondrous sayings of the Buddhas and Patriarchs as proof, taking them for the Buddha-dharma] This chapter teaches cultivation within freedom from thought, which is investigating apart from mind, intention, and consciousness, seeking solely the settling of a single thought. If, in the course of this inquiry, you deliberate over the profound words and wondrous sayings of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, you fall into the discriminating mind and run directly counter to seeing the nature. Hence it was said above that in inquiry one must “lay down all at once one’s own body and mind, one’s world, and all former worldly truths, customary words,
Buddhist views and understanding
.” Below it is further cautioned: “In short,
have no concern for anything — sage or ordinary, deluded or awakened

, but seek solely the settling of a single thought.” The profound words and wondrous sayings of the Buddhas and Patriarchs are the finger pointing at the moon; the true Buddha-dharma is the bright moon in the sky. [The shell of having nothing to do] A shell of idleness, referring to the empty stillness of sitting without delusive thoughts and without gazing and investigating. Chan Master Fayan said: “You must rouse your spirits fiercely, raise a huatou, and investigate it by day and by night, grappling with it. You must not sit inside the shell of having nothing to do, nor sit dead on the meditation cushion. If stray thoughts grow more and more as you struggle with them, gently put them down, get off the cushion and walk a while, then return to the cushion. Open your eyes, clench your fists, straighten your spine, and raise the huatou again as before. You will then feel cool and clear, as if a ladle of cold water had been poured into a pot of boiling soup. Working in this way, there is sure to be a time when you arrive home.” (From the Outline of the Buddhas and Patriarchs)

“In short, have no concern for anything — sage or ordinary, deluded or awakened — but seek solely the settling of a single thought. Pursue it until it is utterly exhausted and cut off; after a long while you will naturally see your original face, like meeting your own father at the crossroads, with no further need to ask others about it.”

In short, have no concern for anything — sage or ordinary, deluded or awakened — but seek solely the settling of a single thought. Pursue it until it is utterly exhausted and cut off; after a long while you will naturally see your original face (see the mind and the nature), like meeting your own father at the crossroads, certain beyond doubt, with no further need to ask others whether this is indeed seeing one’s original face (seeing the mind and the nature).

[Like meeting one’s own father at the crossroads] Like meeting one’s own father at the crossroads, whom one cannot mistake. A metaphor for knowing with certainty that this is the original face, without error.

“Seen in this way, this matter is originally everyone’s own proper concern, with nothing at all extraordinary about it. Practitioner of the Way, if you are truly and genuinely concerned with the great matter of birth and death, try starting from here — I will certainly not deceive you.”

Seen in this way, this matter is originally everyone’s own proper concern, with nothing at all extraordinary about it. Practitioner of the Way, if you are truly and genuinely concerned with the great matter of birth and death, try starting from here (cultivation within freedom from thought) — I will certainly not deceive you.
